title: Defeated, then victorious
hook: the Romans have been defeated, and within a few years will win (30:2–4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spider's house, and your line was not the spider's house. What thin thing did you catch yourself reaching for? Day five hundred thirty, and a new surah.

In the early six hundreds, the two great empires of the world were at war: the Romans of Constantinople, whom we now call the Byzantines, and the Persians. And the Romans were losing badly. The Persians took Syria, then, in 614, Jerusalem, then Egypt. In Mecca, far from all of it, people followed the news. The Muslims, a small persecuted group, felt a sympathy with the Romans, who were Christians, people of a scripture. Many of the Quraysh sided with the Persians. And then a surah began with a headline.

Surah Ar-Rum, the Romans, the thirtieth. Pickthall: "The Romans have been defeated". In the nearer land, the verses go on, and after their defeat they will be victorious, within a few years. The phrase is bid' sinin. Bid' in Arabic means a handful, a small number, usually understood as between three and nine. And then: on that day the believers will rejoice in God's help. At the time it sounded impossible. The Roman empire looked finished. A report in Tirmidhi says Abu Bakr was so sure of it that he made a wager with some of the Quraysh, before wagers like that were forbidden, and when the time came, he won it. History did turn. In the 620s the emperor Heraclius campaigned deep into Persian territory, and by the end of the decade the Persians had sued for peace. Many commentators note that the Muslim victory at Badr, which the believers did rejoice over, fell in those same years, so the verse's rejoicing has been read both ways. Scholars have discussed exactly which events fit the dates. But the verses aren't really about empires. The very next lines say: God's is the command, before and after. And then the surah widens out into a long meditation on signs: night and day, rain on dead earth, the cycle of life. A defeat, the verses say, isn't the end of a story. It's a chapter. The defeated can win, within a handful of years, and the One who turns it is the same One who brings green out of dead ground every spring.
screen: `THE ROMANS HAVE BEEN DEFEATED.` · `BID' SININ: A HANDFUL OF YEARS.` · `ABU BAKR'S WAGER.` · `GOD'S IS THE COMMAND, BEFORE AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hope in a reversal. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one place in your life where you're losing right now. A fight with your health, a project that keeps failing, a relationship that's gone cold, a habit that keeps winning. Don't pretend it isn't a defeat. Just hold it, and then let yourself imagine the same scene a handful of years from now, turned around. What would be different? What small step points that way? If you pray, you can ask for help with it. The bell holds the time.
Defeated. The opening of Ar-Rum: the Romans have been defeated, and after their defeat they will win, within a handful of years. Today's word.
Your line: within a few years. Today, take the small step you pictured toward the reversal, even if it's tiny. Day five hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Muslims read the opening of Surah Ar-Rum as a prophecy fulfilled in the Byzantine recovery under Heraclius, and as a reminder that the outcome of events belongs to God.

fork.setup: you're in Mecca. the Romans have lost Jerusalem. the verse says they'll win within a few years. the Quraysh laugh. what does Abu Bakr do?
options: make a wager that it will come true.
fork.reveal: a report in Tirmidhi says he wagered with some of the Quraysh, before such wagers were forbidden, and won.

original.note: Arabic: 'the Romans have been defeated', the opening words of surah thirty after alif, lam, mim.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old news story about an empire.
what it means: a defeat named plainly, a reversal promised within a handful of years, and God's command over both.
what a scholar hears: bid' sinin, three to nine years; the Persian conquest of Jerusalem in 614 and Heraclius's victories in 622–628; Abu Bakr's wager in Tirmidhi 3193.

sources.ref: Qur'an 30:3–5 (victory within a few years; God's command)

notes: Pickthall 30:2 quoted from memory; confirm. Pickthall renders bid' sinin in 30:4 as 'within ten years', I believe; the script paraphrases with 'within a few years', matching the outline. Confirm.
Dates: Persian capture of Jerusalem 614; Heraclius's campaigns 622–628 and the peace c. 628–630. Confirm.
Abu Bakr's wager: Tirmidhi 3193 cited from memory; confirm. The note 'before wagers like that were forbidden' follows the commentaries.
Some commentators tie the believers' rejoicing to Badr (624), others to Hudaybiyyah or to the Roman victory itself; script says 'read both ways'. Confirm.
